questions.q: A student says an asteroid is a star. What is the best correction?
choices: A star is always smaller than a car.
Every asteroid has its own bright light.
An asteroid is a space rock, not a star.
Asteroids stay in one place in the sky.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 1 of the original A1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why can two asteroids look very different in size?
choices: All asteroids are bigger than Earth.
Some are small, while others are very large.
All asteroids are the same size.
An asteroid grows whenever it moves.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 1 of the original A1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why do scientists take more than one picture of a space rock?
choices: They need to make the rock brighter.
The same photo cannot be saved.
They want to move the rock themselves.
They can watch where the object goes.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 2 of the original A1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: You want to see an asteroid that is very far away. What would help?
choices: A large telescope can show distant objects.
A book about the weather is enough.
You must wait for the rock to land.
You need to go to a museum first.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 2 of the original A1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: How is Ceres different from many other asteroids?
choices: It is the only object near Mars.
It makes its own light.
It is round, while many others have uneven shapes.
It travels through the ocean.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 3 of the original A1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why might a museum show a very old meteorite?
choices: It is a piece of space rock that reached Earth.
It is a star that has stopped shining.
It is a picture taken by a telescope.
It is a new rock made in a laboratory.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 3 of the original A1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: A small rock enters the air around Earth but never reaches the ground. What probably happens?
choices: It becomes a new planet.
It burns up while moving through the air.
It stops moving around the Sun forever.
It turns into a large moon.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 4 of the original A1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Why do scientists watch the sky even when very big hits are rare?
choices: They know a big rock will land tomorrow.
They want to stop the Sun from moving.
They can see every space rock without a telescope.
They want to learn more and help keep people safe.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 4 of the original A1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: Two space rocks follow different paths. What word describes these paths?
choices: Telescopes are paths used by scientists.
Orbits are the paths objects follow around the Sun.
Meteorites are roads between planets.
Stars are the names of all space paths.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 2 of the original A1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.

questions.q: After reading about asteroids, what is a useful next step for a student?
choices: Assume every space rock is dangerous.
Stop learning because the sky is too far away.
Call every light in the sky an asteroid.
Look at the night sky and ask questions about space.
questions.explanation: The answer is supported by paragraph 4 of the original A1 reading passage; other choices exaggerate or contradict the described evidence or its implications.
